nameStory: Spotted medick gets its name from the distinctive dark spots that appear on its heart-shaped leaflets, making it easy to distinguish from other clovers. The word 'medick' comes from ancient Greek, referring to plants from Media (modern-day Iran), though this particular species is actually native to the Mediterranean region.
description: Spotted medick is a low-growing annual plant in the pea family that spreads along the ground in a mat-like pattern. It produces small yellow flowers typical of legumes and has three-part leaves with characteristic dark spots. The plant rarely grows more than a few inches tall but can spread outward up to a foot or more. Like other legumes, it has the ability to fix nitrogen in the soil through a partnership with beneficial bacteria.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three-part clover-like leaves with distinctive dark purple or black spots in the center of each heart-shaped leaflet - these spots are your best clue for identification

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny bright yellow pea-type flowers arranged in small clusters of 2-5 blooms, each flower only about 1/8 inch long with the classic legume shape

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, spreading mat that hugs the ground rather than growing upright, with stems that feel somewhat succulent and smooth to the touch

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Develops distinctive coiled, spiny seed pods that look like tiny snail shells and feel rough when rubbed between your fingers

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaflets have a soft, slightly fuzzy texture and often show fine teeth along their edges when examined closely

habitat: Look for spotted medick in disturbed areas like roadsides, parking lot edges, and waste ground, particularly in coastal areas where it's most likely to be found. It thrives in well-drained, often poor soils and full sun exposure. In New England, it's quite rare with only a few documented sightings, most likely in urban or disturbed coastal locations.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges with the characteristic spotted leaves appearing first, making this the best time to spot the diagnostic leaf markings.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering time with small yellow blooms visible, followed by the development of the distinctive coiled, spiny seed pods.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to die back as an annual, but the coiled seed pods may persist and can still be found for identification purposes.
seasonality.winter: As an annual plant, spotted medick dies completely and won't be visible above ground during winter months.

funFact: Spotted medick's seed pods are natural works of art - they coil into perfect spirals with spines, looking like tiny medieval maces, and this intricate design helps the seeds stick to passing animals for dispersal!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small clovers, but the dark spots on the leaves are a dead giveaway - no other common clover has these distinctive markings. If you see spots, you've got spotted medick!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'heart clover,' this isn't a true clover (Trifolium) but rather a medick in the same legume family. The heart-shaped leaflets with their romantic appearance have made this plant popular in European folklore as a symbol of love.
compareHints: Unlike black medick which has tiny black dots in the center of yellow flowers and no leaf spots, spotted medick's defining feature is the dark spots on its leaves. Alfalfa grows much taller and has purple or blue flowers rather than yellow, plus lacks the distinctive leaf spotting that makes spotted medick unmistakable.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Black medick differs from its cousin alfalfa by being much smaller and more prostrate, while alfalfa grows tall and upright.
Alfalfa is larger and more upright than its cousin black medick, which stays low and has yellow flowers instead of purple ones.
